summary: Gives sets of test cases for HMAC used with the RIPEMD-160 and RIPEMD-128 hash functions. Implementers can use them to check their code. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It is an answer key to check that a program computes a certain kind of digital fingerprint correctly.

subtitle: Test vectors for checking HMAC message authentication with RIPEMD hash functions.

tldr.problem: Implementations of HMAC using RIPEMD-160 and RIPEMD-128 hash functions need a way to verify that their code is correct.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2286 provides seven test cases for each of HMAC-RIPEMD160 and HMAC-RIPEMD128, each with a key, input data, and the expected message authentication code output.
tldr.outcome: Developers can run these tests against their implementation to confirm it produces the correct authentication codes.

facts.label: Number of test cases per algorithm

today: RFC 2286 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. RIPEMD and HMAC remain in use, though SHA-based HMAC algorithms like HMAC-SHA-256 are more commonly used for new systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 2286 provides test cases (also called test vectors) for implementations of HMAC-RIPEMD160 and HMAC-RIPEMD128. HMAC is a method for constructing a message authentication function (a keyed hash, or digital fingerprint) from an underlying hash function. RIPEMD-160 and RIPEMD-128 are cryptographic hash functions that can be used as the underlying hash in the HMAC construction.

These test cases are designed to serve as a conformance test: implementers can run their code against these cases and check that they get the same results, verifying their implementation is correct.
sections.plainLanguage: This document lists correct answers for a particular type of fingerprinting computation. If your code gives these same answers, it is working right.

sections.title: Test Case Structure and Format
sections.content:
Each test case specifies a key, the input data to be authenticated, and the expected digest (the output). Some test cases include a digest-96 value, which is the first 96 bits (12 bytes) of the full digest, representing truncation to 96 bits.

Keys and data are given either as hexadecimal numbers (prefixed with '0x') or as ASCII character strings in double quotes. When data is specified as an ASCII string, the HMAC computation does not include the trailing null character. For cases where data or key is specified as a repeated byte (such as '0xdd repeated 50 times'), the implementer must expand this to 50 copies of that byte.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test case says 'use this key and this data, and you should get this answer'. Some also test using only part of the answer.

sections.title: HMAC-RIPEMD160 and HMAC-RIPEMD128 Test Cases
sections.content:
RFC 2286 provides seven test cases for HMAC-RIPEMD160 and seven for HMAC-RIPEMD128. The test cases cover a range of scenarios: short keys and short data, longer data, keys longer than the hash function's block size (requiring the key to be hashed first), and truncation of the output.

Test case 1 for HMAC-RIPEMD160 uses a 20-byte key and the data 'Hi There', and produces a 20-byte digest. Test case 5 also shows the digest-96 value (the truncated version). Test cases 6 and 7 use keys that are 80 bytes long, which exceeds the 64-byte block size, forcing the implementation to hash the key first.
sections.plainLanguage: The seven tests include short inputs, long inputs, and very long keys. They cover the typical things an implementation needs to handle.

sections.title: Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC includes C source code showing how to implement HMAC-RIPEMD160, assuming the underlying RIPEMD-160 library has an API similar to the MD5 library described in RFC 1321. The code initializes inner and outer padding values, XORs the key with these padding values, and performs two hash operations (inner hash of padded key and data, then outer hash of padded key and inner result).

To adapt the code for HMAC-RIPEMD128, only the hash function calls need to change from RMD160 to RMD128 (and constants like digest size). The HMAC construction itself remains identical.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC shows working code that implementers can use as a reference. It takes a key and data, does some special padding, and hashes everything twice.
